title: Implement a first-in-first-out queue using only two stacks. Also discuss implementing a stack using two queues.
shortTitle: Implement Queue using two Stacks / Stack using two Queues

s1_definition.profdef: This is a design problem that converts one data structure into another using only its opposite. A queue is First-In-First-Out while a stack is Last-In-First-Out, so you use two stacks — an inbox and an outbox — and transfer elements between them to reverse the order when needed. The amortized cost of each operation stays constant because every element moves between the two stacks at most once.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh processes customer cheques at National Bank of India, but he only has two in-trays that behave like stacks, where the last cheque dropped in is the first picked up. Customers must be served in the order they arrived. So he drops every new cheque into the "incoming" tray. When he needs to serve the oldest customer, if the "serving" tray is empty, he flips the whole incoming tray into the serving tray, which reverses the order so the oldest is now on top. He keeps serving from the serving tray until it empties, then flips again.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use an inbox stack for pushes and an outbox stack for pops, and only flip the inbox into the outbox when the outbox is empty.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a design problem that converts one data structure into another using only its opposite. A queue is First-In-First-Out while a stack is Last-In-First-Out, so you use two stacks — an inbox and an outbox — and transfer elements between them to reverse the order when needed. The amortized cost of each operation stays constant because every element moves between the two stacks at most once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh processes customer cheques at National Bank of India, but he only has two in-trays that behave like stacks, where the last cheque dropped in is the first picked up. Customers must be served in the order they arrived. So he drops every new cheque into the "incoming" tray. When he needs to serve the oldest customer, if the "serving" tray is empty, he flips the whole incoming tray into the serving tray, which reverses the order so the oldest is now on top. He keeps serving from the serving tray until it empties, then flips again.

**One line to remember:** Use an inbox stack for pushes and an outbox stack for pops, and only flip the inbox into the outbox when the outbox is empty.

sections.s2_technical:
A stack reverses order on transfer, so moving everything from one stack into another flips First-In-Last-Out into First-In-First-Out. You keep two stacks: an `inbox` where every new element is pushed, and an `outbox` from which elements are served.

The enqueue operation is simple: always push onto the inbox. For example: `public void enqueue(T item) { inbox.push(item); }`. This is constant time, no transfer needed.

The dequeue operation checks the outbox first. If the outbox is empty, you pour the entire inbox into it, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top of the outbox. For example: `if (outbox.isEmpty()) { while (!inbox.isEmpty()) outbox.push(inbox.pop()); } return outbox.pop();`. If the outbox already has elements, you just pop from it directly.

The key insight is amortized analysis. A single dequeue might trigger a full transfer that costs linear time, but each element is moved from inbox to outbox exactly once in its lifetime. Spread across all operations, the average cost per operation is constant. The crucial rule is to only transfer when the outbox is empty; transferring on every dequeue would break the ordering and ruin the complexity.

The mirror problem, a stack using two queues, is less efficient. To keep LIFO behavior you make either push or pop costly. The common approach makes push costly: enqueue the new element, then rotate the queue by dequeuing and re-enqueuing all older elements so the newest sits at the front. A senior nuance is that the two-stacks-for-a-queue solution is the practically useful one with constant amortized cost, while two-queues-for-a-stack always has one linear operation and is mostly an interview exercise.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, cheque-clearing requests must be processed strictly in arrival order, which is a queue requirement. But the legacy clearing module exposes only stack-like buffers. We must present a fair First-In-First-Out queue to the business while internally using two stack buffers. This is exactly how "queue using two stacks" works — one stack collects arrivals and the other serves them in reversed, correct order.

Problem 2 — Under load, requests arrive in bursts and are served in bursts. We want the amortized cost to stay low rather than paying a reversal on every single serve. This is exactly the "only flip when the outbox is empty" rule — each cheque is transferred once, keeping the average cost constant even during bursts.

The mini-project builds a `ChequeQueue<T>` backed by two `ArrayDeque` stacks with `enqueue`, `dequeue`, and `peek`, a `ChequeClearingService` that uses it to process cheques in order with logging, and a runnable demo that interleaves arrivals and clearings.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is submissions CHQ-001, CHQ-002, CHQ-003, then a clear, then CHQ-004, then three clears.

Step 1: Submit CHQ-001, CHQ-002, CHQ-003. All three are pushed onto the inbox. The inbox from bottom to top is CHQ-001, CHQ-002, CHQ-003, so CHQ-003 is on top. The outbox is empty.

Step 2: Clear next. The outbox is empty, so the whole inbox is flipped into the outbox. Popping CHQ-003, CHQ-002, CHQ-001 from the inbox and pushing each onto the outbox leaves the outbox with CHQ-001 on top. The dequeue pops CHQ-001, which is the oldest. Correct FIFO order.

Step 3: Submit CHQ-004. It is pushed onto the inbox. The outbox still holds CHQ-002 and CHQ-003 with CHQ-002 on top.

Step 4: Clear next. The outbox is not empty, so no flip happens. It pops CHQ-002, the oldest remaining. 

Step 5: Clear next. The outbox pops CHQ-003.

Step 6: Clear next. The outbox is now empty, so the inbox flips into the outbox, moving CHQ-004 to the outbox top. It pops CHQ-004. Every cheque was served exactly in arrival order.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  enqueue CHQ-001,002,003
    │ push onto inbox
    ▼
  inbox: [001,002,003]   outbox: []
    │
  dequeue() → outbox empty → FLIP
    │ pop inbox → push outbox (reverses)
    ▼
  inbox: []   outbox: [003,002,001]  (001 on top)
    │ pop outbox → CHQ-001 oldest
    ▼
  enqueue CHQ-004 → inbox:[004]  outbox:[003,002]
    │ dequeue() → outbox NOT empty → no flip → pop 002
    ▼
  continue: 003, then flip again for 004
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Queue using Two Stacks ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Adapter: two LIFO stacks adapted into a FIFO queue       │
  │  Lazy transfer: flip only when outbox empty (amortized)   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: ChequeQueue is the FIFO structure; Service orchestrates│
  │  O: generic <T> — reusable for any element type           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   ChequeQueue<T>                      │
  │  - inbox:  Deque<T>  (newest on top)  │
  │  - outbox: Deque<T>  (oldest on top)  │
  │  + enqueue(T): void                   │ O(1)
  │  + dequeue(): T                       │ amortized O(1)
  │  + peek(): T                          │ amortized O(1)
  │  - shiftIfNeeded(): void              │ flip when outbox empty
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Amortized proof: each element moves inbox→outbox exactly once.
  n enqueues + n dequeues = 2n pushes + 2n pops total = O(n) → O(1) avg.

  Contract for dequeue():
    Pre:  queue not empty (else NoSuchElementException)
    Post: returns and removes the oldest element (FIFO)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Implementing a queue with two stacks is a lesson in how reversing order with one structure gives you the behavior of its opposite. A stack is Last-In-First-Out and a queue is First-In-First-Out, so I keep two stacks, an inbox and an outbox. Every enqueue simply pushes onto the inbox in constant time. A dequeue serves from the outbox, and only when the outbox is empty do I pour the entire inbox into it, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top and is served first.

The subtle point that interviewers listen for is the amortized analysis. A single dequeue can trigger a full transfer that is linear in that moment, but each element is only ever moved from the inbox to the outbox once in its whole lifetime, so averaged over all operations the cost per operation is constant. The rule that makes this work is transferring only when the outbox is empty; flipping on every dequeue would both break the ordering and destroy the complexity.

The mirror problem of building a stack from two queues is worth mentioning as a contrast. There is no way to get amortized constant cost for both operations, so you make either push or pop linear, usually by rotating the queue so the newest element sits at the front. It is a fine interview exercise but far less practical than the two-stacks queue.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this pattern in the cheque-clearing module, where cheques must be processed strictly in arrival order but the legacy buffers behaved like stacks. The inbox collected arrivals and the outbox served them in corrected order, and because clearing happens in bursts, the lazy-flip rule kept the average cost low even when a batch of cheques arrived and was cleared together.
